title: The fifth Veda: dance as worship
hookLine: the gods ask Brahma for something everyone can see and hear, and he makes dance and drama a Veda
carry: natya, the fifth veda: dance offered to god
tomorrow: how can chopping vegetables be worship?

cards: The old manual of drama, the Natya Shastra, opens with sages asking its teacher, Bharata, where all this came from. He tells a story.
Long ago the world had slid into greed, anger and trouble, and the gods went to Brahma with a request. The Vedas, they said, are not heard by everyone.
Make something else: something to see and to hear, for every kind of person. A fifth Veda.

teach.b: Brahma sat in thought and drew from all four. From the Rig Veda he took the words. From the Sama Veda, song.
From the Yajur Veda, abhinaya, the art of acting it out. From the Atharva Veda, rasa, the taste of feeling.
He called it the Natyaveda and gave it to Bharata, and later in the telling Shiva adds his fierce dance, the tandava, and Parvati her graceful one. Here's the teaching inside the origin story.

teach.h: BOW TO THE EARTH, OFFER THE DANCE.
teach.b: In Hinduism, dance and drama aren't just entertainment beside religion. They were made as a Veda, a way of knowing, open to anyone who can watch.

That's why classical dancers begin by bowing: touching the floor, which many explain as asking the earth's pardon for stamping on her, and offering the dance to the deity. On the stage, the hands do the speaking.

A later dancers' manual, the Abhinaya Darpana, lists them one by one: pataka, the flag; mukula, the bud; hamsasya, the swan's beak. One shape can be a cloud, a forest or a blessing, and the story tells you which.

It also gives a chain dancers love to quote, in paraphrase: where the hand goes, the eyes follow; where the eyes go, the mind; where the mind goes, the feeling; and where the feeling goes, rasa arises.
A hand moving in the lamplight, and a whole room tasting devotion. So when a girl in a New Jersey studio rehearses a poem about Krishna, by her tradition's own story, she's studying a Veda.

how: In classical Indian dance forms such as Bharatanatyam and Odissi, dancers begin with a bow to the earth and an offering to the deity, then use named hand gestures (hastas) and facial expression to tell stories, often of the gods; the Natya Shastra tells how Brahma made drama and dance a fifth Veda.

words from the rig, song from the sama, acting from the yajur, feeling from the atharva.

games.q: a cousin says classical dance is 'just culture, not religion.' by the Natya Shastra's story, what fits?
o: Brahma made it a fifth Veda, a way of knowing, and dancers offer it to God.
right, it was invented to entertain kings.
it only becomes religious if a priest blesses the stage.
games.why: the gods asked for a Veda everyone could see and hear; Brahma made natya. that's why dancers bow to the earth and offer the dance.

practice: Begin the way dancers do: touch the floor lightly with your right hand, then bring it to your eyes. Make pataka, the flag: hand flat, fingers together, thumb bent in, in front of your chest.
Move it slowly out to the right and back, then to the left, eyes following the hand. If you pray, let the movement be your offering; if not, just notice whether the mind follows the eyes.

wordCard.voice: The mudras. In dance, hastas: hand shapes that tell a story, where the hand leads and the eyes, the mind and the feeling follow.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: natya, drama and dance together. The Natyaveda is the fifth Veda Brahma made.
